title: Trumpet
reference_instrument: University of Iowa MIS Bb trumpet (Bach 180S37 Stradivarius, 1987, per MISBbtrumpet.html)
summary: A Bb trumpet with the valves up, played by a lip valve whose pitch is never an input: the note is the lock the loop finds between the lip and the bore, and only the open harmonics of the instrument are valid. The bore is the 34-station profile (mouthpiece cup and throat, backbore, leadpipe, cylinder, bell) published with Tournemenne and Chabassier (2019), copied digit for digit from the openwind example file; its valves are straightened, so the valve loops, slides and ports are absent. The lip is the outward-striking mode of the artificial latex lips Cullen (2000) measured on a trombone-size mouthpiece (her embouchure 19, the tightest of 20), because no trumpeter's lip is published; it is a trombone-rig artificial lip, not a trumpeter's, and playability entered the choice (the looser embouchure 7 the trombone uses would not start D5 below 27.5 kPa nor hold it below about 21 kPa). The graded sound is the radiated pressure of the actual bell disk at a baffled point 1.524 m away, not the mouthpiece pressure. Nothing was fitted to the Iowa recordings; the pre-stress of each held note was set from the emergent pitch of a first render against equal temperament (a player tuning an embouchure), and no pitch, note or frequency is an input. The mouth pressure of each held note is a cited player input: 3.5 times the threshold K f of Fletcher and Tarnopolsky's (1999) trumpet players with K = 7 Pa/Hz, the loud-playing pressure they measured (5.7, 8.6, 11.4 and 14.4 kPa for Bb3, F4, Bb4 and D5); at those pressures this model's notes are quieter and duller than they measured, as the lip-source item below records, and the earlier renders at a constant 14 kPa, which sat nearer the measured level but with a shank fundamental 11 dB too strong, are superseded. It is a population stand-in (a different trumpet from the recorded Bach 180S37), and that the stations were measured from a real commercial trumpet is as reported and not verified by this lane.
physics_present: fs-couple brass_loop: a one-degree-of-freedom outward-striking lip island advanced by exact held-force propagation, a Bernoulli aperture solved implicitly with the mouthpiece junction, closing on the bore's reflectance

fs-duct multimodal transfer-matrix bore with exact Bessel viscothermal loss, realized as a passive causal line by a convergence ladder over the line length, terminated in the flanged-piston radiation load; the mouthpiece cup and throat are geometry in the bore, not a lumped volume

an outlet observer built from the same duct: the mouth volume flow per incident wave from the same transfer-matrix chain, differentiated and delayed by the Rayleigh integral over the real 0.061 m bell disk to a baffled receiver, so the graded sound is radiated pressure, not mouthpiece pressure

a lip tension gesture (pre-stress) and a blowing-pressure gesture on the shared canonical schedule format, with held-note, tension-sweep and pressure-ramp recipes in render.sh (the ramps measure the oscillation threshold, extinction pressure and hysteresis of this model)

diagnostic taps in music_render lip, none of them an input to a note: --impedance scans the passive bore (multimodal and plane-wave input impedance peaks and heights, and the analytic radiated-per-internal transfer of a baffled piston on axis), --mouthpiece-wav writes the internal mouthpiece pressure, and the sidecar carries per-0.1 s lip-closure and mouthpiece-level windows; the observer chain was checked against that analytic transfer and agrees to 1.2 dB through partial 8 on F4, so the radiation path is not where the spectrum is lost
physics_missing: the valves: the bore file is straightened, so the valve loops, tuning slide, valve slides and ports are absent, and only the open-valve harmonic series (concert Bb3, F4, Bb4, D5) is valid; valve combinations are not rendered. The library can already switch between pre-built valve-path bores (BrassVoice combinations, SetValve events, the ValveInsertedLength gesture target), but music_render lip holds one bore and its schedule accepts only blowing pressure and pre-stress, so no card can reach it. What is missing is data for one specific trumpet: each valve's loop length, the straight port-to-port length it bypasses, the loop bore and the valve block's station along the bore. No open source with those numbers was found on 2026-10-30; equal-tempered loop lengths would be the pitch target and not a measurement, and are not used

the recorded trumpet: the Iowa instrument is a Bach 180S37 and no numeric bore of it was found, so this is a population stand-in; the measured-from-a-real-trumpet origin of the stations is as reported, the paper text could not be opened (HAL bot challenge) and the file states no maker, method or uncertainty

a trumpet player's lips: the lip is an artificial latex lip pair measured on a trombone-size mouthpiece (cup 25.5 mm against this trumpet's 16.8 mm), only its outward-striking mode, with a channel width and rest gap that are not a trumpeter's; no trumpet-player lip mass, width or rest gap is published (Yoshikawa 1995, Richards 2003 and the Stevenson and Campbell work were looked for and none gives a complete set). Embouchure 19 was chosen over 7 for the cup diameter (7's 12 mm channel is 47 percent of the rig cup but 71 percent of this one) and because playability entered the choice: D5 on embouchure 7 started only at 27.5 kPa and stopped near 20.8 kPa, so a 21 kPa hold fell silent, because a single loose lip row scaled only by pre-stress puts every upper note at the extinction edge, and not because the lip resonance missed the bore mode (diagnostic sweeps speak the Bb4 and D5 windows on embouchure 7 at 25 kPa)

intonation: the stand-in bore's own passive impedance peaks lie 41 to 62 cents flat of the equal-tempered open series for partials 3 to 6, so the notes are flat of equal temperament until the lip is tightened, and the hold pre-stresses (0.93, 1.42, 1.9, 2.42) were chosen to bring the emergent pitch to the note; how a real Bach 180S37 would sit is unknown

the level and the spectrum (diagnostic, the earlier embouchure-19 holds at a constant 14 kPa, now superseded by holds at the Fletcher and Tarnopolsky pressures), compared with Resch et al. (arXiv 1611.01025), who measured harmonic SPLs at the SHANK of a Bb Barcelona BTR-200LQ trumpet played forte and 16 cm outside its bell (their Fig 4, digitized from the raster to about 1 to 2 dB; their notes sound 51 cents sharp of equal temperament, and it is a different trumpet). Our tap is at the lip junction (cup rim) and their microphone is at the shank (x = 83.7 mm in the station table, where the radius steps 4.2 to 4.64 mm; the throat-to-shank radius ratio 0.43 matches their 'about 0.4'); the bore's own passive cup-to-shank transfer is +1 dB at 232 Hz and -3 to -18 dB from 465 Hz up, so the two must be compared at the same place, and earlier versions of this card that compared the cup rim with their shank (the internal spectrum '22 to 24 dB too steep', 'shape right, level 10 dB high at every harmonic', transfer '3 to 5 dB high at the fundamental and 7 to 12 dB low above') are withdrawn. At the shank the Bb3 hold is within 3 dB of their measured harmonic levels at partials 2, 3 and 5 to 11 and 12 dB too strong at the fundamental (partials 4 and 12 fall on a notch of the cup-to-shank transfer and are 9 dB low), so its total level, 177 dB against their 167.2, is the fundamental alone; the Bb4 hold is 4 dB high at the fundamental, 5 to 11 dB low at partials 2 to 4 and 16 dB low at partials 5 and 6 (total 171 dB). The shank-to-bell transfer, from an independent re-implementation of the plane-wave bore checked against the playing loop's own scan to within 1 dB, has a mean absolute error of 4.8 dB (Bb3) and 3.6 dB (Bb4) against the bell-over-shank ratio they measured, but a tilt from 240 Hz to 2.9 kHz of 30 dB against their 42.5 dB (Bb4 22.6 against 31.6): ours is 5 to 9 dB too high at partials 1 to 3 and 3 to 7.5 dB too low above 1.9 kHz. A spherical-wave aperture at the bell mouth (43 degree half-angle; closed form checked against the numerical Rayleigh integral) changes it by under 1.2 dB, an ideal open end by under 4 dB, and the unflanged load is refused above ka 1; the low-partial excess is of the size of the 6 dB between a baffled and an unflanged mouth at low ka, which is not evaluated. The lip closes in 87 to 97 percent of the 0.1 s chunks, and the passive impedance peaks are not too high against the one published calculated pair (no missing-loss evidence). Blowing-pressure ladder (F4, cup rim): 163.7, 168.4, 171.5 and 175.9 dB at 5, 8, 11 and 14 kPa, with the internal fourth partial falling from -21.9 to -27.7 dB re the fundamental between 14 and 8 kPa, so lowering the drive dulls the spectrum; those renders were at 14 kPa, above the 3.3 to 3.9 times threshold (about 6 to 14 kPa for these notes) at which Fletcher and Tarnopolsky's players played loudly; the holds now use 3.5 times 7 Pa/Hz times f (see the lip-source item for what those pressures give). Untested candidates: nonlinear propagation, which is absent (at these amplitudes the shock-formation distance, about 0.7 to 1.1 m by the standard estimate, is shorter than the tube), and the multimodal field at the bell mouth

the lip source (diagnostic, Bb3 holds at 14 kPa from 33 cents flat to 63 cents sharp of equal temperament): the fundamental at the shank stays 11.5 to 12.3 dB over Resch's while the bore's impedance at it changes by 16 dB, so bore support is not the cause; it tracks the blowing pressure (internal level 163.7, 168.4, 171.5 and 175.9 dB at 5, 8, 11 and 14 kPa for F4). The lip flow rebuilt from the tapped pressure and the playing loop's own impedance (its gap maximum and mean agree with the render's own statistics to about 15 percent) is closed for about 45 percent of the period, opens in about 0.65 ms and closes in about 1.4 ms, the same family as Bromage's (2007) measured trombone opening-area waveforms (closed 22 to 40 percent of the period for Bb2, F3 and D4, read from his Fig 4.45, closing slower than opening), but its flow harmonics are weak (n = 2 to 8 are 14 to 19 dB under the fundamental), so the harmonic content at a matched fundamental is too low. The lip aperture area here is width times gap (area exponent 1); Bromage measured area proportional to height^q with q 1.2, 1.3, 1.6 and 1.9 for a trombonist at Bb1, Bb2, F3 and F4 mezzo-forte (artificial mouth 1.0 to 1.6): a measured difference, not yet implemented. Against Fletcher and Tarnopolsky (1999), who measured blowing pressure and radiated level for trumpet players (read from their figures, about 1 dB; different players differ by about 3 dB): their thresholds are about 7 Pa/Hz (4 to 8 for three players), this lip's are 21 to 33 Pa/Hz at onset on a slow ramp and 8 to 12 Pa/Hz at extinction (Bb3, F4, Bb4, D5: onset 5.7, 11.7, 9.7 and 13.0 kPa, extinction 2.3, 3.0, 3.7 and 7.0 kPa). At the pressures their players used for the same notes (Bb3 2.8 to 6, F4 3.3 to 9, Bb4 4 to 10 kPa) the radiated A-weighted level at 1 m is 12 to 21 dB under player NH's (living room) and about 10 dB under the anechoic player GC's (F4), it rises about 8 dB per doubling of pressure where theirs rises about 15 and then 3, and the frequency above which its envelope is more than 20 dB under the peak is 1.0 to 2.3 kHz where they measured 6 to 13 kHz at 4 to 7 kPa. At a matched shank fundamental (Bb3 at 5 kPa, Bb4 at 10 kPa) partials 2 to 8 are 10 to 24 dB under Resch's, so the deficit is already there 8 cm from the lip and is not only a propagation effect (they attribute the high-frequency extension of the radiated spectrum to nonlinear propagation, which is absent here). The lip opening is within the measured range at matched pitch, so no saturation law is implemented (their 1 mm is a modelling estimate): at the cited pressures the steady gap maximum of the render is 2.4, 1.4, 1.25 and 1.0 mm for Bb3, F4, Bb4 and D5 (maximum open area 21, 13, 11 and 9 mm2 with the 9 mm width; at 14 kPa 5.5, 2.3, 1.5 and 1.0 mm), against the maximum travel of a trombonist's top lip measured by Stevenson (2009, Table 4.2, about 1 mm: 3 to 4 mm non-brassy and 6 mm brassy at Bb3, at most 1 to 2 mm non-brassy and 1 to 5 mm brassy at F4) and the trombone open areas Bromage (2007, Fig 4.46) measured (8 to 27 mm2 at D4 and 16 to 58 mm2 at F3, non-brassy to brassy). These are trombone lips; no trumpeter's opening was found (Yoshikawa 1995 was not available), so the comparison cannot exclude a trumpet-specific difference
turbulence and breath noise of the lip jet: none is modelled, so the render is a clean harmonic signal and its harmonic-to-noise ratio is far above the recordings' (the hnr_db measure of the grading)
the mouthpiece as a separate measured part: the cup and throat come from the same station table, and their agreement with a Bach 7C or any named mouthpiece is not established

a clock that reaches the bell's radiation ceiling: the flanged radiation load is admitted only to ka 20, so the render runs on a 32 kHz clock (not 48 kHz) and everything above the receiver's resolved band (6.9 kHz) is unmodelled

the mouth-flow radiation transfer is the plane-mode image of the duct, not the multimodal one the reflectance line uses; and the microphone is an on-axis point: the player's bell orientation, the cardioid KM 84 directivity and any room are not modelled; the receiver is a baffled half-space piston, so a real unflanged bell radiates about 6 dB less at low ka, which is not evaluated: the open source for the unflanged mouth (Silva, Guillemain, Kergomard, Mallaroni and Norris 2009, arXiv 0811.3625) gives the planar-mode reflection coefficient and end correction to ka 3.8 but no directivity or far-field transfer
breath-warmed and humidified bore gas, wall vibration, nonlinear propagation and shock formation at forte (the source of brassiness), mutes, and the player's tonguing and vibrato
a same-specimen or same-model impedance pair, so the passive chain is checked only against published population data
